Question: Tom’s age is \(T\) years, which is also the sum of the ages of his three children. His age \(N\) years ago was twice the sum of their ages then. What is \(\frac{T}{N}?\)
Solution:
The useful distinction is that Tom’s age decreases by \(N\) when we look back \(N\) years, while the sum of three children’s ages decreases by \(3N\). Since their current age sum is \(T\), their earlier age sum was \(T-3N\), and Tom’s earlier age was \(T-N\).

At that time his age was twice their total, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
T-N&=2(T-3N),\\
T-N&=2T-6N,\\
T&=5N.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(N\) years ago refers to a past time, \(N>0\). Dividing by \(N\) gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{T}{N}=5},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
